summary: South Fox Island Light, in northern Lake Michigan, was lit in 1867 and kept by keepers until 1958. Its 1934 steel tower came from Georgia. The station is state land, reached by boat.

light.characteristic: fixed red, varied by a red flash every two minutes (as listed in 1899)

lens.note: L. Sautter & Co. fourth-order Fresnel per LighthouseFriends; the Board's 1899 report says fourth order

structures.note: 39 ft (11.9 m) from base to lantern centre per the U.S. Lighthouse Society record; FILA's history gives 45 ft to the top of the ventilator.
Cast-iron skeletal tower built 1905 on Sapelo Island, Georgia; taken down in 1933 and reassembled on South Fox Island in 1934. FILA gives 104 ft.

access.note: Reached by boat or air only. Grounds open; dwellings and towers closed (LighthouseFriends).

stay.note: Camper Keeper Program begun in 2015, for stays of several weeks while helping with upkeep (LighthouseFriends). Check with the association for dates.

facts.agency: Michigan Department of Natural Resources owns the southern 115 acres and the light station (LighthouseFriends; FILA). Most of the rest of the island is private (Terry Pepper, 2003).

events.note: Congress appropriated $18,000 on 2 March 1867
Keeper Henry J. Roe first lit the light on 1 November 1867
Board fence, 320 feet long, built against drifting sand and snow
About 600 feet of walkway built; the Board's report says the work was done by the keeper
10-inch steam whistle in operation from 10 December 1895
Brick oil house for kerosene, replacing lard oil
Assistant keepers' dwelling replaced with red brick
Four keepers towed a disabled launch with five persons on board to a wharf
Illuminant changed from oil to incandescent oil vapour
Keepers helped transport a sick woman to medical attention (Bulletin); LighthouseFriends also records a disabled boat towed to a fishing tug
Hyacinth's launch towing motor boat No. 63 was caught in the breakers and wrecked; the first officer drowned
Light electrified; steam fog signal replaced by a Tyfon air signal
Skeletal tower from Sapelo Island, Georgia, reassembled beside the brick tower
Fog signal discontinued
Light converted to automatic operation; last keeper Allen P. Cain leaves
Last crew leaves; the fourth-order lens goes to Old Presque Isle Light, Lake Huron
Fourth-order lens from the lantern moved to Old Presque Isle Light, Lake Huron
Automatic light shut down; electronic navigation had made it obsolete
Southern 115 acres passed to the Michigan Department of Natural Resources
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, 26 August 2021

corrections.why: FILA's history says the automatic light was shut down in 1968; 1959 is the year the last crew left. The 1934 'discontinued' date in the U.S. Lighthouse Society record refers to the brick tower, not the station.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: FILA measures 45 feet from the base to the top of the ventilator; the U.S. Lighthouse Society record gives 39 feet from the base to the centre of the lantern. The measures differ, so the two figures do not contradict each other.
The 1934 'discontinued' date in the U.S. Lighthouse Society record is for the brick tower replaced by the Sapelo tower. The light station itself ran until 1968 (FILA).

notes_for_editor: NOT VERIFIED: The NRHP nomination (NRHP 100006861, npgallery PDF) returned a placeholder image, so the story does not use it. The Lighthouse Board reports for 1866 to 1890 are not in the local corpus; the 1867 appropriation and the first lighting rest on FILA, Terry Pepper and LighthouseFriends (three secondary sources that agree). The fog-signal cost differs between reports: $5,500 in the 1891-1892 volume recommendation and $5,600 in the 1893 authorisation; the 1895 appropriation is $5,500. Not explained by the sources read. Keeper end dates conflict. The archive roster (cite 1) ends McCormick in 1923, Green in 1934 and Frank M. Bourissau in 1934; LighthouseFriends (cite 2) runs them to 1924, 1940 and 1937. Both lines are kept. The Bulletin's 1922 account names Emil C. Johnson first assistant and Dame second; the archive roster has Dame first assistant from 1921 and no Johnson. Johnson is added from the Bulletin. Lewis Bourissau's roster entry is printed as 'Lewis (Louis) G. Bourissau'; Terry Pepper spells Bourisseau and LighthouseFriends Lewis Bourissau. The Bulletin 1916 OCR prints 'Hay H. Buttars'; the Bulletin index and the archive roster give Ray H. Buttars. Ray H. Buttars is used. The Commissioner of Lighthouses' 1921 table (scan p. 667) was read from OCR; its fiscal-year heading is not legible, so the story does not give a year for it. The 1914 Bulletin item is dated 'On July 8' within the 1914 volume; the year is taken from the volume. LighthouseFriends cites a 2002 Detroit Free Press article for the 1953 log; that article was not read. The 1953 log line is quoted through LighthouseFriends. The 1916 LighthouseFriends rescue (disabled boat towed to a fishing tug) is not in the Bulletin; it is kept with attribution. The 1910 Vega item (Calumet News) gives no place on the island and no link to the light; kept as a wreck with that caveat. FILA's history gives the light's end as 1968, its station page gives 1969 for decommissioning; the 1971 transfer is described as a transfer in FILA's history and a purchase in its station page. The story uses the history's wording. The record's 'deactivated 1959' conflicts with FILA's 1968; a correction is proposed for human review. The record's stay note (keeper program) is confirmed only through LighthouseFriends; FILA's own volunteer page was not read. Allen P. Cain's connection ended in 1958, before the 1960 cut-off, so he is named as published sources name him. Terry Pepper's 2003 statement that most of the island is privately owned is not updated. The developer is not named. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-27: fiscal-year labels corrected against the volumes. The 1891-1892 'volume' is two reports: scan p. 167 is the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891; scan p. 494 (sidewalk, FY1892) is the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1892. The 1893 and 1895 citations are also now labelled by fiscal year (scan p. 171 in the FY1893 report; scan p. 335 in the FY1895 report). The 1914 Bulletin keepers were checked on the page image (PDF p. 36: 'William F. Green'). The 1916 page image (PDF p. 35) reads 'Ray H. Buttars' and 'In June'; the OCR read 'Hay H.'; the 1916 index (PDF p. 7) confirms Ray H. Buttars. The 1922 Bulletin (PDF p. 49) names James McCormick, keeper, and Nels Nelson as third assistant; the story does not use Nelson's 1922 entry. The Commissioner's 1921 table names 'Jamea McCormick' in OCR; McCormick is confirmed by the Bulletin and LighthouseFriends. Founding dates disagree: FILA's history gives the Fox Island Education Association 2000 and the Fox Island Lighthouse Association 2004; LighthouseFriends gives 2002 and a 2005 name change. The story states both. The decommissioning year disagrees: FILA's history gives 1968 for the shutdown; FILA's station page gives 1969 for decommissioning. The story states both. The skeletal tower's material disagrees: FILA's history says cast iron; FILA's station page says steel. The story states both. The 1893 Board report gives $5,600 and the 1891 report gives $5,500; a later repeat in the 1894 report reads $5,500 in OCR. The story states the 1891 and 1893 figures and the 1895 appropriation. The story no longer uses the 1899 wording 'fixed red with a red flash'; it quotes the Board's own phrase. Atmosphere: the sentence 'The fog signal was the keepers' heaviest work' had no source and was removed. The 1968 shutdown is no longer presented as caused by electronic navigation; FILA's own sentence is quoted instead. The 1959 'deactivated' correction stands for human review. Quotations from LighthouseFriends are now limited to the 1953 log sentence and short phrases; the 1866 Board quotation is paraphrased.
